newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler may use reserve for growth moves.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler may use reserve for growth moves.

text.p: Chrysler Corp chairman Robert Eaton said Tuesday the automaker may be able to get through the next recession without dipping into its hefty cash reserve to fund operations, and it could use the reserve to fund growth instead.

Eaton told reporters in a conference call that Chrysler is "getting more and more confident that we can go through the next downturn, largely getting through it on operating earnings, and that would allow us to use a significant portion of our cash reserve for growth opportunities that might just occur during such a downturn, if and when it occurs."

Chrysler said Tuesday its automotive cash reserve stood at $6.95 billion at year-end, compared with $6.89 billion at the end of 1995. The automaker has had a longstanding goal of maintaining a reserve of $7.5 billion.

Eaton declined to elaborate on possible growth uses for the cash reserve, but Schroder Wertheim analyst John Casesa said one move Chrysler could make is to acquire excess vehicle assembly capacity from another automaker that may be hurt by the downturn.
Currently, however, Eaton said there is no industry downturn in sight.
He said 1997 "should be an excellent year."
Chrysler estimates U.S. auto industry sales should reach 15.2 million vehicles in 1997, including medium and heavy trucks, compared with 15.4 million in 1996, he said.
Chief Financial Officer Gary Valade said Chrysler's cumulative share repurchases since 1995 will in 1997 likely surpass the amount of stock it issued in 1991 and 1993 to raise cash for operations.
Chrysler raised about $400 million by offering 40 million shares at $10 each in 1991. It raised $2 billion in 1993 by selling 52 million shares at about $39 each.
Since then, the shares have split two-for-one. They were trading Tuesday at $35.75, up $1.25.
Since its share repurchase programs began in January 1995, Valade said Chrysler has bought back about 112 million shares, or roughly 14 percent of its shares outstanding, at a cost of $3.1 billion.
Chrysler has committed to buying back another $2 billion worth of stock in 1997 and has said it intends to return excess cash above its $7.5 billion reserve target to shareholders.

Chrysler today reported record fourth quarter earnings of $1.09 billion, or $1.51 a share, excluding $279 million in special charges. The results exceeded analysts' consensus estimate of $1.43 a share.
In the fourth quarter of 1995 Chrysler earned $1.04 billion, or $1.33 a share.
